cards.title: The Ship of Theseus
cards.body: Replace every plank of a ship one at a time and you still call it the same ship. Your body swaps out most of its cells over the years, and your opinions change even faster.
cards.chew: What part of you, if it changed, would make you a different person?

cards.title: Amor fati
cards.body: Nietzsche's idea: don't just put up with what happened to you. Love it, because every bad day was part of the road that made you.
cards.chew: Which rough stretch of your life are you secretly glad about now?

cards.title: The eternal return
cards.body: Imagine you had to live this exact life again, every moment in the same order, forever. Nietzsche used it as a test: would that thought crush you or thrill you?
cards.chew: What would you change this week so the answer is 'thrill'?

cards.title: The examined life
cards.body: Socrates thought most people sleepwalk through their days on autopilot and borrowed opinions. Examining your life means asking why you want what you want.
cards.chew: Name one thing you want that you've never actually questioned.

cards.title: Wu wei
cards.body: Taoists praise 'effortless action': moving with the grain of a situation the way water flows around rocks. It's the feeling of a run where you stop thinking and just ride.
cards.chew: Where in your life are you forcing something that would go better if you flowed?

cards.title: The present is all you get
cards.body: The past is a memory and the future is a guess. Every experience you'll ever have happens in a now that's always a few seconds wide.
cards.chew: What's happening right now that you're not noticing?

cards.title: The view from nowhere
cards.body: Thomas Nagel asked how we can see the world from no particular perspective. Zoom out far enough and your worst embarrassment is a pixel on a speck in a galaxy.
cards.chew: Does zooming out make your problems feel smaller, or your life feel smaller? Can it be both?

cards.title: Hedonic treadmill
cards.body: Get the new board, the raise, the bigger place, and within months it feels normal. Happiness snaps back to a baseline almost no matter what you add.
cards.chew: What's something that has never stopped making you happy?

cards.title: Memento mori
cards.body: Roman generals in parades supposedly had someone whisper 'remember you will die.' The point wasn't gloom. It's that a short life makes today expensive.
cards.chew: If you had one year, what would you stop doing tomorrow?

cards.title: Sonder
cards.body: The realization that every stranger in traffic has a whole life as vivid and complicated as yours, and you're an extra in theirs.
cards.chew: Who did you see today who's the main character of a story you'll never know?

cards.title: The dichotomy of control
cards.body: Epictetus split the world in two: what's up to you (your effort, your response) and what isn't (weather, other people, results). Stress lives in mixing them up.
cards.chew: What are you worrying about this week that sits in the second pile?

cards.title: Premeditatio malorum
cards.body: Stoics rehearsed things going wrong ahead of time: the lost job, the injury, the canceled trip. Not to be gloomy, but so nothing knocks them flat.
cards.chew: What's one setback you could plan a calm response to now?

cards.title: Two-minute rule
cards.body: If something takes under two minutes, do it now. Little undone tasks pile up and quietly drain your energy.
cards.chew: What tiny task have you been carrying around in your head for days?

cards.title: Strong opinions, loosely held
cards.body: Pick a direction and commit hard, but drop it the moment the evidence changes. Being decisive and being open aren't opposites.
cards.chew: What opinion of yours would you drop if you found out you were wrong?

cards.title: Chesterton's fence
cards.body: Before you tear down a fence in the middle of nowhere, find out why someone built it. Old rules sometimes look dumb until you learn what they prevented.
cards.chew: What 'dumb' rule at work might be guarding against something?

cards.title: The map is not the territory
cards.body: Your plan, your org chart and your mental picture of a person are all simplified maps. Reality always has more detail than the map.
cards.chew: Where are you trusting a map over what's actually in front of you?

cards.title: Second-order thinking
cards.body: Ask 'and then what?' The first effect of a decision is obvious. The second and third effects are where the surprises live.
cards.chew: Take a decision you're weighing and ask 'and then what?' three times.

cards.title: Done is a feature
cards.body: A finished thing that's 80% good beats a perfect thing that lives in your head. You can't improve what you never shipped.
cards.chew: What could you ship this week at 80%?

cards.title: Reply to the best version
cards.body: When someone says something that annoys you, answer the smartest version of their point, not the dumbest. It changes how arguments go.
cards.chew: Who could you steelman instead of strawman this week?

cards.title: Sympatheia
cards.body: Marcus Aurelius kept reminding himself that everyone is connected, like limbs of one body. What's bad for the hive is bad for the bee.
cards.chew: Who is quietly carrying something heavy that you could lighten?

cards.title: Dogs have no idea
cards.body: Your dog thinks you leave every morning to go hunting and come back with groceries. Honestly, it's not that far off.
cards.chew: What do you think your pets believe your job is?

cards.title: Cats are landlords
cards.body: Your cats let you live in their house in exchange for food, cleaning, and the occasional chin scratch, which they can revoke at any time.
cards.chew: Which of your animals would be the worst roommate as a human?

cards.title: Confident wrong
cards.body: Somewhere right now, a man is explaining to a ski instructor how to ski.
cards.chew: What's a topic you're dangerously confident about?

cards.title: The meeting that could've been an email
cards.body: Every meeting has a ghost email living inside it, trying to escape.
cards.chew: What's the shortest possible version of your next meeting?

cards.title: Bread is a hostage situation
cards.body: A bag of bread twist-tie is a tiny puzzle box designed by someone who hates breakfast.
cards.chew: What everyday object would you redesign out of spite?

cards.title: Disc golf physics
cards.body: The disc will skip off a tree, ricochet off a rock, and land exactly where you couldn't putt from. Every time. It's not luck. It's personal.
cards.chew: What sport or game do you swear is rigged against you?

cards.title: Adulthood
cards.body: Being an adult is mostly saying 'we should hang out soon' for six years.
cards.chew: Who have you been 'getting together soon' with for too long?

cards.title: The snooze button
cards.body: Hitting snooze is negotiating with a hostage taker who is also you, and you always lose.
cards.chew: What's your most pointless daily negotiation with yourself?

cards.title: Card game math
cards.body: Every card player is one draw away from either godhood or quitting forever. There is no in-between.
cards.chew: What's your best 'topdeck of destiny' story?

cards.title: Socks
cards.body: Somewhere there's a planet populated entirely by single socks, and they're all wondering where their other half went too.
cards.chew: What mundane mystery would you want solved before you die?

cards.title: Gamer time
cards.body: 'Five more minutes' in gamer time is a unit of measurement roughly equal to two hours and one missed dinner.
cards.chew: What's your most dangerous 'just one more'?

cards.title: Experience machine
cards.body: Robert Nozick offered a machine that gives you any experiences you want, perfectly real-feeling, forever. Most people say no. Why, if it feels identical?
cards.chew: Would you plug in? What would you miss that you can't name?

cards.title: Boltzmann brain
cards.body: Some physicists joke that it's statistically likelier for a lone brain with fake memories to pop into existence than a whole universe. You might be one, remembering this card.
cards.chew: How do you know your memories happened?

cards.title: The teleporter
cards.body: A teleporter scans you, destroys you, and builds an exact copy on Mars. The copy feels like you and remembers your breakfast. Did you travel, or die?
cards.chew: Would you step in? Would you if it saved a 6-hour drive?

cards.title: Mary's room
cards.body: Mary knows every physical fact about color but has lived in a black-and-white room. When she walks out and sees a red apple, does she learn something new?
cards.chew: Is there something you 'know' but haven't actually experienced?

cards.title: The trolley, but you're the trolley
cards.body: Every choice you make sends the future down one track and not another. You're always pulling a lever, just slowly.
cards.chew: What 'lever' did you pull this year without noticing?

cards.title: Newcomb's box
cards.body: A perfect predictor puts $1M in a box only if it predicted you'd take just that box, and leaves $1K in another box. It already decided. Do you take one box or both?
cards.chew: Are you a one-boxer or two-boxer, and what does that say about you?

cards.title: Sorites heap
cards.body: Remove one grain from a heap of sand and it's still a heap. Repeat. When exactly does it stop being a heap? Nobody can say.
cards.chew: What change in your life happened grain by grain?

cards.title: Simulation tax
cards.body: If we're in a simulation, the cheapest way to run it would be to render only what someone is looking at. Quantum physics behaves a little suspiciously like that.
cards.chew: If you found out it was a sim, what would you do differently tomorrow?

cards.title: Fermi's question
cards.body: The universe is huge and old, so where is everybody? Either life is rare, it doesn't last, or it's hiding. Every answer is kind of wild.
cards.chew: Which answer scares you the most?

cards.title: Roko's sandwich
cards.body: Imagine a future AI that only rewards people who brought it a sandwich. You now know about it. Are you obligated? (No. But you thought about it.)
cards.chew: What weird idea lives in your head rent-free?

cards.title: Send it
cards.body: The worst version of the line you were scared of is still more fun than standing at the top for 20 minutes.
cards.chew: What are you standing at the top of right now?

cards.title: 1% better
cards.body: Get 1% better every day and you're about 37 times better in a year. Get 1% worse and you're almost at zero. Tiny daily stuff compounds.
cards.chew: What's one 1% thing you can do today?

cards.title: Bails are reps
cards.body: Every skater has eaten it hundreds of times on a trick before landing it once. The slams weren't failure. They were the practice.
cards.chew: What are you bailing on that just needs more reps?

cards.title: Start ugly
cards.body: The first version of anything good was bad. The first board you rode, the first code you wrote, the first drawing. Ugly is how you start.
cards.chew: What could you start ugly today?

cards.title: Future you is watching
cards.body: In ten years, a version of you will look back at this exact week. Give them something to be proud of, or at least something funny to tell.
cards.chew: What would future you thank you for doing tonight?

cards.title: Energy, not time
cards.body: You can't make more hours, but you can stop spending your best energy on stuff you don't care about.
cards.chew: What drains you that you could cut or delegate this week?

cards.title: The boring middle
cards.body: Every project has an exciting start, a satisfying finish, and a long boring middle where most people quit. That's where it's won.
cards.chew: What project of yours is in the boring middle?

cards.title: Ask anyway
cards.body: The worst answer you'll get is no, and 'no' is where you already are if you never ask.
cards.chew: What do you want to ask for but haven't?

cards.title: Small wins stack
cards.body: Finishing one small thing gives you momentum to finish the next. Momentum is a cheat code.
cards.chew: What's the smallest finishable thing on your list?

cards.title: Plato's cave
cards.body: Plato imagined prisoners chained in a cave their whole lives, watching shadows on a wall and taking them for reality. One breaks free, sees the sun, and comes back to tell the others. They laugh at him and would rather keep the shadows.
cards.chew: What shadow did you once take for the real thing?

cards.title: The useless tree
cards.body: Zhuangzi tells of a huge, gnarled tree whose wood was too twisted to build anything with, so no carpenter ever bothered to cut it down. Being useless is exactly why it grew so old. Not everything good in your life has to be productive.
cards.chew: What do you love doing that has no practical point at all?

cards.title: The second arrow
cards.body: The Buddha compared pain to being struck by an arrow, then pointed out that we usually shoot ourselves with a second one: the worrying, blaming and replaying. The first arrow often can't be dodged. The second one is mostly up to you.
cards.chew: What second arrow have you been firing at yourself lately?

cards.title: Sisyphus, smiling
cards.body: In Greek myth, Sisyphus is doomed to roll a boulder uphill forever, only to watch it roll back down. Albert Camus argued he could still be happy. The meaning isn't waiting at the top of the hill; it's in owning the push.
cards.chew: What's your boulder, and could you learn to love the push?

cards.title: Hanlon's razor
cards.body: Don't blame malice for what carelessness explains. The coworker who ignored your message probably has a pile of other unread ones. Most things that feel like attacks are just people being busy, tired or distracted.
cards.chew: Whose 'rude' move this week might just have been a rushed one?

cards.title: Invert, always invert
cards.body: The mathematician Carl Jacobi advised attacking hard problems by flipping them around. Instead of asking how to have a great year, ask what would guarantee a miserable one. Then stop doing those things.
cards.chew: What's the surest way to wreck next month, and are you already doing any of it?

cards.title: Sunk costs stay sunk
cards.body: You paid for the lift ticket, but the runs are pure ice and you're miserable. That money is gone whether you stay or leave. The only real question is the best way to spend the next three hours.
cards.chew: What are you still doing mostly because you already paid for it?

cards.title: Five-star review
cards.body: To a skateboarder, a 'No Skateboarding' sign isn't a rule. It's a glowing review confirming the ledge is perfect.
cards.chew: What 'no' in your life is secretly a sign you've found a good spot?

cards.title: Cats do science
cards.body: Your cat pushes your pen off the desk while staring right at you. It's not rude, it's research: confirming gravity still works, again, with you as the unpaid lab assistant.
cards.chew: What do you keep re-checking even though you already know the answer?

cards.title: The door always wins
cards.body: A D&D party spends forty minutes planning how to get past one locked door, with disguises, forged letters and a bard distraction. Then the barbarian just kicks it. He rolls a 1, and the door wins.
cards.chew: What simple problem have you spent forty minutes overplanning?

cards.title: Hilbert's hotel
cards.body: Mathematician David Hilbert pictured a hotel with infinitely many rooms, every one of them full. A new guest shows up, so everyone moves to the next room up, and room 1 opens. Full, yet there's still room: infinity plays by its own rules.
cards.chew: Your calendar isn't Hilbert's hotel, so what could move out to make room?

cards.title: The Chinese room
cards.body: John Searle imagined sitting in a room with a rulebook for matching Chinese symbols. Notes slide in, you follow the rules, and perfect Chinese replies slide out, though you don't understand a word. Is a computer doing the same thing, or something more?
cards.chew: How could you prove you understand something, rather than just following the rules well?

cards.title: Monty Hall's doors
cards.body: Three doors, one car, two goats. You pick one, then the host, who knows where the car is, always opens another door to show a goat and offers a swap. Switching wins two times out of three, because your first pick only ever had a one-in-three shot.
cards.chew: Where are you sticking with a first choice just because it came first?

cards.title: The surprise test
cards.body: A teacher announces a surprise test next week. A student reasons it can't be Friday, since by Thursday night it wouldn't be a surprise, so it can't be Thursday either, and so on back to Monday. Feeling clever, he skips studying, and Wednesday's test surprises him completely.
cards.chew: What did you rule out as impossible right before it happened?

cards.title: Eyes on the line
cards.body: Mountain bikers learn it fast: the bike goes where your eyes go. Stare at the rock you're scared of and you'll ride straight into it. Look at the gap past it and you'll flow right through.
cards.chew: What rock are you staring at so hard that you're steering toward it?

cards.title: The spotlight effect
cards.body: In a classic study, students made to wear an embarrassing T-shirt into a room guessed about half the people there noticed. Only about a quarter did. Everyone else is too busy starring in their own life to watch you fall.
cards.chew: What would you try in public if you knew hardly anyone was watching?

cards.title: Recovery is training
cards.body: Muscles don't get stronger during the workout. Training stresses them, and they rebuild stronger while you rest and sleep. Skipping recovery isn't hardcore; it's skipping the part where you actually improve.
cards.chew: When did you last rest on purpose instead of by collapsing?

cards.title: Spend your skill points
cards.body: In most RPGs you can't max every stat. The strongest builds pick a few skills and pour everything into them, while spreading points evenly makes a hero who's fine at everything and great at nothing.
cards.chew: If you only had three skill points to spend this year, where would they go?
